title: Market & coffee
mission: Buying, haggling, and being fed: the souq with its kilo-arithmetic and neighbor-gambit, the coffee that cannot be refused (correctly), and the food words old enough to be Hebrew's cousins. Arc 1 ends where Palestinian life convenes — around the scale and the tray.
sources: Forms cross-checked against Madrasa dictionary and Living Arabic Project (Levantine)
Urban Palestinian koine (Jerusalem/Ramallah); native-speaker review pending — low-confidence items avoided

lessons.title: At the market
lessons.canDo: I can buy produce at the souq — price it, doubt it, haggle it down a shekel, and walk off with the right change.

blocks.body: The souq is a listening gym disguised as shopping: prices fly, quantities double, and the haggle has fixed moves you can learn like chess openings. First move: never accept the first price. Second move: invoke the neighbor.

example.en: I'm going to the market — need anything?

items.note: Also the economy itself: السوق واقف — business is dead. Unit 2's herd-driving root, arrived at its destination.

cognate.note: s-w-q, to drive herds — to where? To market. Your שוק and the Palestinian سوق are the same destination of the same cattle drive.

example.en: The vegetable seller opens early.

items.note: Collective: the green stuff. The vegetable man is the خضرجي — that ـجي is the Ottoman job-suffix, like كهربجي the electrician.

example.en: Fruit is expensive this season.

items.note: The singular فاكهة is rarely heard — the fruit stand thinks in plurals.

example.en: How much is a kilo of tomatoes?

items.note: كيلو ونص، كيلو وربع — Unit 2's fraction system now sells produce. بندورة, by the way, is pomodoro — Italian tomatoes that learned Arabic.

example.en: Give me two cucumbers and one tomato.

items.note: The counting word for things you can hold: حبة، حبتين، تلات حبات. At the pharmacy it's a pill.

example.ar: خبز طازة، طالع هلّق من الفرن.
example.en: Fresh bread, just out of the oven.

cognate.note: Turkish taze went two directions: the Palestinian طازة and the Israeli slang טאזה. Same freshness, same Ottoman delivery truck.

example.en: Everything's gotten expensive.

items.note: Unit 1's protest chant, now at the stall. Also affection: يا غالي — 'you precious one.' The market and the heart share a vocabulary.

example.en: Onions are cheap these days.

items.note: Cheap in price; said of a person, an insult. Mind the register.

example.en: The vendor swore it was fresh.

items.note: The فعّال profession pattern: باع sells → بياع seller, ساق drives → سواق driver. Hear the doubled middle and you've found someone's job.

example.en: The regular customer gets a better price.

items.note: Plural زباين. Being a زبون دايم earns credit, gossip, and the good tomatoes from under the table.

blocks.title: Six shekels?!
blocks.situation: Morning souq. Tomatoes, an outraged counter-offer, and the oldest move in the game: the neighbor's price.

lines.speaker: زبون
lines.ar: صباح الخير. البندورة كيف اليوم؟
lines.en: Morning. How are the tomatoes today?

lines.speaker: بياع
lines.ar: صباح النور. طازة من الصبح يا عمي.
lines.en: Morning. Fresh from dawn, sir.

lines.speaker: زبون
lines.ar: بكم الكيلو؟
lines.en: How much per kilo?

lines.speaker: بياع
lines.ar: ستة شيكل.
lines.en: Six shekels.

lines.speaker: زبون
lines.ar: ستة؟! غالي يا زلمة. عند جارك بأربعة.
lines.en: Six?! That's steep, man. Your neighbor has them at four.

lines.speaker: بياع
lines.ar: جاري بضاعته من مبارح. هاي قطفة اليوم.
lines.en: My neighbor's stock is from yesterday. This is today's picking.

lines.speaker: زبون
lines.ar: خلص، حط كيلوين. وشوية خيار كمان.
lines.en: Fine — two kilos. And some cucumbers too.

lines.speaker: بياع
lines.ar: تكرم. شو كمان؟ عنا عنب طازة.
lines.en: You got it. What else? We've got fresh grapes.

lines.speaker: زبون
lines.ar: لأ، بكفي هيك اليوم.
lines.en: No — that's enough for today.

lines.speaker: بياع
lines.ar: صحتين وعافية. خمسطعش شيكل كله.
lines.en: Enjoy in health. Fifteen shekels for everything.

questions.prompt: The vendor's opening price per kilo:

questions.why: Invoking the neighbor's price — the souq's oldest opening.
Freshness beats price — هاي قطفة اليوم.
خمسطعش — the ـطعش teens from the number gym, now costing you money.

items.en: How much is a kilo of tomatoes?
These are fresh goods — from this morning.

points.explanation: Arabic counts 'two' with a suffix, not a word: كيلوين two kilos, حبتين two pieces, يومين two days. Hear ـين on a noun and delete the word 'two' from your search — it's already in there. (You've been hearing it since سنتين in Unit 2.)

examples.en: Two kilos of tomatoes and two cucumbers.
We waited two hours at the checkpoint yesterday.

points.explanation: Two interchangeable price questions: بكم (by-how-much) and قديش حق + suffix (how much is its due). Answers come verbless and bare: ستة شيكل. Pricing is arithmetic spoken aloud — no sentence required.

examples.en: How much is a kilo of grapes today?
How much is this local cheese?

items.story: s-w-q: drive the herd (ساق، سواق) and you arrive at the market. The Israeli שוק and the Nablus سوق are the same word at the end of the same cattle path — and both still shout.
Ottoman Turkish taze, 'fresh,' was left behind in both languages when the empire packed up: طازة on the Palestinian stall, טאזה in Israeli slang. One empire, two souvenirs, same tomatoes.

lessons.title: How much is it really?
lessons.canDo: I can handle the money layer: prices, change, the tab, the scale — and know when بكفي.

blocks.body: Under the haggling sits the machinery: مصاري and فراطة, the دفتر where debts live, the scale whose honesty is the vendor's whole name. This is also a lesson in roots: حق is price, truth, and right at once — worth contemplating on the walk home.

example.en: What's the price of the olives?

items.note: One word, three lives: the price (حقه عشرة), the right (حقي!), the being-right (حقك عليّ — you're right / my fault, the argument-ender).

cognate.note: ḥ-q-q: Arabic kept truth, right, and price; Hebrew carved the statute — חוק. What's owed, what's true, and what's law — one root adjudicates all three.

example.en: I've got no money on me today.

items.note: THE Levantine money word — from the old مصري (Egyptian) coinage. فلوس also circulates.

example.ar: عندك فراطة؟ ما معي إلا مية.
example.en: Got change? I've only got a hundred.

items.note: From فرط — money broken into bits. عندك فراطة؟ is half of all market dialogue and all of all serveece dialogue.

example.en: Half the neighborhood buys on credit.

items.note: دَين debt vs دِين religion — same letters, one vowel apart, and the dictionary keeps them as neighbors on purpose. Hebrew דין (judgment) is the family's third brother.

example.en: Put it on the tab — I'll settle up Thursday.

items.note: Unit 1's حسب (according to) grown into a noun. الحساب لو سمحت — the check, please.

cognate.note: ḥ-š-b: حساب and חשבון are the same reckoning — the bill, the account, the settling. עושה חשבון and بعمل حساب even share the idiom.

example.en: Put the tomatoes on the scale.

items.note: Root w-z-n, weight — Hebrew מאזניים swapped the و for an א, same instrument. An honest ميزان is the vendor's entire reputation; the Quran uses it for cosmic justice.

example.en: Put them in a strong bag for me.

cognate.note: One root, two sizes: the Arabic كيس carries the shopping; the Hebrew כיס is the pocket. Both exist to hold المصاري — and both are where it disappears.

example.en: The stock arrived this morning.

items.note: The haggling lever: بضاعة اليوم vs بضاعة مبارح. You heard the vendor wield it against his neighbor.

example.en: That's enough, thanks.

items.note: Impersonal verb — 'it suffices.' Alone it's the brake pedal: بكفي! With a suffix it budgets: كيلو بكفيني لأسبوع.

example.en: Pick for yourself, sir — it's all in front of you.

items.note: The vendor's trust move: choose your own. From نقي, pure — picking is purifying. The doubled middle again: make-pure → hand-select.

blocks.title: Abu al-Abed's notebook
blocks.brief: Thirty years behind a vegetable stall: where the goods come from, who pays cash, who pays at month's end, and why the scale is never wrong. The market's social economics in eight sentences.
preQuestions: Where do his goods come from?
How does he track the customers who buy on credit?
What does he say the market really is?

transcript.speaker: أبو العبد
transcript.ar: أنا أبو العبد، بياع خضرة من تلاتين سنة.
transcript.en: I'm Abu al-Abed — a vegetable seller for thirty years.

transcript.speaker: أبو العبد
transcript.ar: بفتح بسطتي الساعة خمسة الصبح، قبل كل السوق.
transcript.en: I open my stall at five in the morning, before the whole market.

transcript.speaker: أبو العبد
transcript.ar: البضاعة بتيجي من الأغوار: بندورة، خيار، كوسا.
transcript.en: The goods come from the Jordan Valley: tomatoes, cucumbers, zucchini.

transcript.speaker: أبو العبد
transcript.ar: الأسعار طالعة، والناس معها مصاري أقل.
transcript.en: Prices keep climbing, and people have less money.

transcript.speaker: أبو العبد
transcript.ar: في زباين بشتروا بالدين — بكتب الحساب بدفتر صغير.
transcript.en: Some customers buy on credit — I write the account in a little notebook.

transcript.speaker: أبو العبد
transcript.ar: واللي ما معه، بستنى عليه. آخر الشهر بسدد.
transcript.en: And whoever can't pay — I wait. End of the month, he settles.

transcript.speaker: أبو العبد
transcript.ar: الميزان عندي صادق. هاي تجارة وهاي سمعة.
transcript.en: My scale is honest. That's business, and that's reputation.

transcript.speaker: أبو العبد
transcript.ar: السوق مش بس بيع وشرا — السوق ناس.
transcript.en: The market isn't just buying and selling — the market is people.

questions.prompt: How long has Abu al-Abed been selling vegetables?
questions.why: تلاتين — the ـين tens ending. The number gym never closes.

questions.prompt: Where do his goods come from?
questions.why: الأغوار — the Jordan Valley, the West Bank's farm belt.
The دفتر — the notebook that holds half the neighborhood's months.
صادق — honest. The ص-د-ق truth-root from Unit 1, weighing vegetables now.

items.en: What's the price of this cheese?
I've got no money on me — I'll pay tomorrow.
Got change? I've only got a hundred.
I buy on credit and settle at the end of the month.
Put the vegetables in the bag.

points.explanation: بكفي is impersonal: it-suffices. Bare, it ends things: بكفي! With object endings it does budgeting: بكفيني (enough for me), بكفينا (enough for us). The politest way to stop a vendor, a host, or an argument.

examples.en: That's enough, bless you.
A kilo of oil lasts us a month.

points.explanation: Three payment states: cash now, عالحساب on the tab, بالدين on credit proper. The دفتر that holds it all is a social institution — Abu al-Abed's notebook carries more trust than most banks.

examples.en: Put it on the tab, Abu al-Abed.
Half the market runs on credit these days.

items.story: ḥ-q-q. Arabic kept the bundle whole: truth, right, price — قديش حقه، هاد حقي. Hebrew carved off the statute: חוק. When a vendor says حقه عشرة and a court says זה החוק, one ancient root is adjudicating both.
ḥ-š-b: the reckoning root from Unit 1's حسب, now a noun on every table: الحساب لو سمحت = החשבון בבקשה. Same bill, same flinch.
The bag and the pocket are one root in two sizes — and the proverbial money vanishes from both: من كيسك means 'out of your own pocket,' exactly where מהכיס שלך hurts.

lessons.title: Coffee, by the rules
lessons.canDo: I can survive Palestinian hospitality with honor: refuse twice, accept the third time, order my coffee سادة, and bless the right hands.

blocks.body: Hospitality here is a formal system with moves and counter-moves: the offer, the refusal (mandatory), the re-offer (inevitable), the surrender (delicious). This lesson teaches the script — and the coffee-sweetness scale that doubles as a personality test.

example.en: Make us some coffee — let's sit a while.

cognate.note: قهوة → Turkish kahve → Venetian caffè → Europe's coffee → Hebrew קפה. The word made a four-century world tour and came home to the Levant wearing a ק.

example.en: We have guests for dinner.

items.note: الضيف ضيف الله — the guest is God's guest, three days by tradition. The whole ض-ي-ف system: ضيف، ضيافة، استضاف.

items.en: here you go; come in; please

example.en: Come in, sit — the house is yours.

items.note: The Swiss-army politeness word: come in / sit / take / after you / here you go. Feminine تفضلي, plural تفضلوا. When in doubt, تفضل.

example.en: Welcome — you've lit up the house.

items.note: The full formula: أهلاً (you've come to family) وسهلاً (onto easy ground). The reply to the reply: نورتوا — 'you brought the light.'

cognate.note: The אהלן Israelis text each other is the first half of this formula, clipped and borrowed. Here it comes with its other half — and with the obligation to actually feed you.

example.en: Health and wellness on you!

items.note: Literally 'two healths' — the dual from Lesson 1, blessing your plate. The reply: على قلبك — 'and on your heart.'

example.en: Tea with mint or with sage?

items.note: Winter runs on شاي ومرمية (sage tea). The host's opening gambit is always the binary: قهوة ولا شاي؟

example.en: No sugar, please.

cognate.note: Sanskrit śarkarā rode through Persian and Arabic سكر into every European tongue and Hebrew's סוכר. Sweetness is humanity's oldest supply chain — and your tea is its terminus.

example.ar: قهوة سادة، زي ما بحبها سيدو.
example.en: Bitter coffee, the way grandpa likes it.

items.note: The coffee scale: سادة bitter → وسط/مظبوطة middle → حلوة sweet. Ordering سادة earns silent respect from every Abu anything.

example.en: They invited us for Friday lunch.

items.note: Unit 2's عزومة is this verb's child. عزمني على قهوة — minimal invitation, maximal obligation.

items.en: bless your hands (thanks to the cook)

example.en: Bless your hands — what food!

items.note: THE compliment to whoever cooked: may your hands stay safe. To a man: يسلمو إيديك. The reply: وإيديك — and yours.

blocks.title: Coffee, three rounds
blocks.situation: A guest drops by Umm Samir's. Watch the choreography: offer, refusal, counter-offer, capitulation — performed by both sides in full knowledge of the ending.

lines.speaker: أم سمير
lines.ar: تفضل، اقعد. شو بتشرب؟
lines.en: Come in, sit. What will you drink?

lines.speaker: ضيف
lines.ar: ولا إشي والله، مش لازم.
lines.en: Nothing at all, really — no need.

lines.speaker: أم سمير
lines.ar: مش معقول! بيتنا بيتك. قهوة ولا شاي؟
lines.en: Out of the question! Our house is yours. Coffee or tea?

lines.speaker: ضيف
lines.ar: خلص، قهوة. بس سادة لو سمحتي.
lines.en: Fine — coffee. But unsweetened, please.

lines.speaker: أم سمير
lines.ar: سادة؟ زي أبوي الله يرحمه. والكنافة وين رايحة؟
lines.en: Bitter? Like my father, God rest him. And where's the knafeh going?

lines.speaker: ضيف
lines.ar: لا لا، كنافة لأ. والله القهوة بكفي.
lines.en: No no — not knafeh. Really, coffee is plenty.

lines.speaker: أم سمير
lines.ar: يا زلمة حطيتها قدامك. صحتين!
lines.en: Man, I've already put it in front of you. Sahtein!

lines.speaker: ضيف
lines.ar: طيب… حبة صغيرة. يسلمو إيديكي.
lines.en: Fine… a small piece. Bless your hands.

lines.speaker: أم سمير
lines.ar: صحة وعافية. وخد معك لمرتك كمان.
lines.en: To your health. And take some home for your wife too.

lines.speaker: ضيف
lines.ar: خلص، استسلمت. أهلك كرماء يا أم سمير.
lines.en: That's it — I surrender. Your family wins, Umm Samir.

questions.why: Round one is always a warm refusal. Accepting immediately is a rookie tell.

questions.prompt: How does he take his coffee?
Who else drank it that way?

questions.why: Round three: accept 'a small piece.' The dance, completed with honor.
Hospitality's encore: you leave with provisions whether you like it or not.

items.en: Come in, sit — the house is yours.
I take my coffee bitter — no sugar.
Who invited you all to dinner?
I ate so much. Bless your hands, grandma.

points.explanation: Hospitality speaks in imperatives that aren't orders: تفضل, اقعد, اشرب — and كول 'eat!' (the imperative of أكل drops the hamza). Feminine: تفضلي، كولي. They sound like commands; they function as gifts. Refusing them politely is the next pattern.

examples.en: Come in, all of you — you've lit up the house.

examples.ar: كول يا زلمة، ما أكلت إشي!
examples.en: Eat, man — you've eaten nothing!

points.ar: لأ والله… → مش لازم… → طيب، حبة صغيرة
points.explanation: The refusal dance is three-round grammar-of-culture: (1) refuse warmly — ولا إشي والله; (2) refuse weakly — والله بكفي; (3) accept minimally — طيب، حبة صغيرة. Skipping to yes reads as greed; holding past three reads as rejection. The host's job is to make round three irresistible; both sides know the score.

examples.en: Nothing, really — no need. (round one, mandatory)
Fine — a small piece. Bless your hands. (round three, inevitable)

items.story: The rare loan that boomeranged: قهوة left Yemen, conquered Istanbul (kahve), Venice (caffè), and the world (coffee) — then arrived in modern Hebrew as קפה, a tourist returning to its home region with a foreign accent.
śarkarā (Sanskrit) → شكر/سكر (Arabic) → sugar, Zucker, סוכר. Arabic was the middleman of medieval sweetness — every European sugar word paid customs in Arabic first.

lessons.title: The food itself
lessons.canDo: I can name the staples — oil, za'atar, the cheese that belongs in knafeh — and follow تيتا's musakhan masterclass.

blocks.body: Food words are the oldest words: the olive, the cheese, and the egg have been cognates since before Hebrew and Arabic were separate languages. This lesson eats its way through the pantry — and ends with تيتا teaching the national dish.

example.en: Get fresh bread from the bakery.

items.note: خبز طابون — from the clay oven — is the musakhan foundation and the smell of every village morning.

example.en: The new year's oil has arrived.

items.note: Unmarked زيت in Palestine means olive oil, full stop — everything else needs an adjective. Families measure the year in tanak (tins) of it.

example.en: Bread, oil, and za'atar — a breakfast of kings.

items.note: Hyssop + sumac + sesame: the national herb. Exam season folklore says it sharpens the brain; the Hebrew זעתר is the same word, borrowed leaf and all.

example.en: The olive harvest is in October.

items.note: The tree is family property across generations; قطف الزيتون (the harvest) is the calendar's anchor — and a season of checkpoint friction, Arc 2 will note.

cognate.note: z-y-t: زيتون/זית, and the oil زيت inside Hebrew's שמן זית. The tree predates both languages, most empires, and every border drawn around it.

example.en: Nabulsi cheese is for knafeh only.

cognate.note: g-b-n: جبنة/גבינה — cheese is cheese, sound for sound. The brined Nabulsi kind is the only one knafeh recognizes as kosher (so to speak).

example.en: Free-range eggs from our neighbor's.

cognate.note: b-y-ḍ: بيض/ביצה. Bonus: the same root paints white — أبيض. The egg named the color, or the color named the egg; either way both languages agreed.

example.en: A plate of hummus and ful in the morning.

cognate.note: Hebrew borrowed the chickpea, the dish, and the eternal whose-is-better argument, all in one word. The argument remains unresolved and load-bearing.

example.en: Friday is maqluba day.

items.note: 'The upside-down one': rice, chicken, fried vegetables — inverted theatrically before the guests. The flip is the ceremony; applause is customary; the قلب root also does hearts and coups.

example.ar: المسخن بده بصل كتير وصبر أكتر.
example.en: Musakhan takes a lot of onion and more patience.

items.note: 'The heated one': taboon bread, mountains of sumac-stained onions, chicken, new oil. THE Palestinian dish — تيتا explains below.

example.en: Nabulsi knafeh, done properly.

items.note: You've chased it since getting lost in Nablus — here's the card. Hot Nabulsi cheese, kataifi, syrup. Settles arguments; starts others.

blocks.title: Teta's musakhan masterclass
blocks.brief: Grandma teaches the national dish, layer by layer — and by the last line it isn't a recipe anymore. Listen once for the ingredients, once for the إضافة chains (خبز طابون، زيت زيتون), and once because it's تيتا.
preQuestions: How much onion — and what's her instruction about shyness?
When did they traditionally make it?

transcript.speaker: تيتا
transcript.ar: تعالوا أعلمكم أشهر أكلة فلسطينية — المسخن.
transcript.en: Come, let me teach you the most famous Palestinian dish — musakhan.

transcript.speaker: تيتا
transcript.ar: أول إشي: خبز طابون. مش أي خبز.
transcript.en: First thing: taboon bread. Not just any bread.

transcript.speaker: تيتا
transcript.ar: بعدين بصل كتير. كيلوين بصل — لا تستحوا.
transcript.en: Then lots of onion. Two kilos of onion — don't be shy.

transcript.speaker: تيتا
transcript.ar: وسماق أحمر، وزيت زيتون من معصرتنا.
transcript.en: And red sumac, and olive oil from our own press.

transcript.speaker: تيتا
transcript.ar: الجاج فوق الخبز، والبصل فوق الجاج.
transcript.en: The chicken on the bread, the onions on the chicken.

transcript.speaker: تيتا
transcript.ar: ساعة بالفرن — والريحة بتوصل لآخر الحارة.
transcript.en: An hour in the oven — and the smell reaches the end of the neighborhood.

transcript.speaker: تيتا
transcript.ar: زمان كنا نعملها بعد قطف الزيتون، بزيت السنة الجديدة.
transcript.en: In the old days we made it after the olive harvest, with the new year's oil.

transcript.speaker: تيتا
transcript.ar: المسخن مش أكلة، يا حبيبي. المسخن موسم، وعيلة، وبلد.
transcript.en: Musakhan isn't a dish, my dear. Musakhan is a season, a family, and a homeland.

questions.why: مش أي خبز — Teta is categorical.
كيلوين — the dual from Lesson 1, و'لا تستحوا' — don't be shy.

questions.prompt: The two signature flavors on top:

questions.why: After the olive harvest — with زيت السنة الجديدة, the new oil.
A season, a family, and a homeland. End of recipe.

items.en: Olive oil from the town press.
Bread, za'atar and oil — a breakfast of kings.
Nabulsi cheese is for knafeh only.
We flipped the maqluba in front of the guests.

items.ar: ال____ بده خبز طابون وبصل كتير.
items.en: Musakhan needs taboon bread and lots of onion.

points.ar: زيت زيتون، خبز طابون، جبنة نابلسية
points.explanation: Food names are noun chains — the إضافة: oil-of-olive, bread-of-taboon, no 'of' spoken, the nouns just touch. Stack Unit 3's nisba on top and the menu writes itself: جبنة نابلسية, كنافة نابلسية. Hear two nouns touching and read the hyphen yourself.

examples.en: Local olive oil from our own press.

examples.ar: جبنة نابلسية وخبز طابون — خلص، عزومة.
examples.en: Nabulsi cheese and taboon bread — that's it, it's a feast.

points.explanation: بلدي — 'of the homeland' — is the food world's highest honor: heirloom, local, real. بندورة بلدي، بيض بلدي، زيت بلدي. One word carrying terroir, nostalgia, and quiet politics: the opposite of imported, industrial, and occupied shelf space.

examples.en: Free-range eggs — yolks that are actually yellow.

examples.ar: هاي بندورة بلدي، ريحتها من بعيد.
examples.en: These are baladi tomatoes — you can smell them from afar.

items.story: z-y-t. The olive predates the split between the languages that argue over it: زيتون/זית, the oil زيت inside שמן זית, even Jabal al-Zaytun/הר הזיתים naming the same hill. The tree was here first and will outlast the argument.
g-b-n: cheese is cheese, sound for sound, from the same dairy root. Knafeh's Nabulsi white and the גבינה צהובה on Israeli toast are estranged cousins at the same wedding.
b-y-ḍ: the egg, and the color white (أبيض) thrown in. Some roots survive everything; breakfast is one of them.
The chickpea crossed over with its name, its tahini, and its whose-is-better war. חומוס is Arabic حمص on an Israeli menu — the most peacefully contested word in the region.

lessons.title: Taste and smell
lessons.canDo: I can describe food — and survive an عزومة — with the senses: delicious, salty, sour, and the fullness that lasts a week.

blocks.body: The palate is pre-Babel: taste, smell, salty, sour, and sated are all words Hebrew and Arabic still share from the deep past. This lesson is the senses — deployed at a dinner where saying 'enough' is only an opening bid.

example.en: What is that delicious smell!

cognate.note: r-y-ḥ — and both grow from روح/רוח, the wind, the spirit. A smell is a small ghost in either language; تيتا's musakhan sends one to the end of the street.

example.en: It tastes like the old days' food.

cognate.note: ṭ-ʕ-m: طعم/טעם. Hebrew stretched it to 'reason, point' — מה הטעם? asks what's the flavor of bothering. A mealtime root doing philosophy.

example.en: The food is delicious — bless your hands.

items.note: The warm everyday word; طيب also serves. Feminine زاكية. Saying it to the cook is not optional.

example.en: The coffee is sweeter than necessary.

items.note: The dialect's all-purpose approval: بنت حلوة، فكرة حلوة، حكي حلو. Antonym at the coffee tray: سادة.

example.en: The soup is a bit salty.

cognate.note: m-l-ḥ: مالح/מלוח, salt ملح/מלח. The mezze table is a cognate display case — and ים המלח keeps the family salt in its name.

example.en: Lemon is sour and honey is sweet.

cognate.note: ḥ-m-ḍ/ץ: حامض/חמוץ — and the pickles prove it: مخلل حامض on one side of the table, חמוצים on the other, the same pucker on every face.

example.ar: والله شبعان، ما بقدر كمان لقمة.
example.en: I swear I'm full — I can't manage one more bite.

cognate.note: ś-b-ʕ: شبعان/שבע — sated. At the عزومة this word is heard constantly and believed never. Declaring it is round one of leaving, which also takes three rounds.

example.en: The kids are hungry — when's lunch?

items.note: جوع is hunger. A word that will return, far heavier, in Arc 3 — here it just means: more maqluba, please.

example.en: Take a bite — just try it.

items.note: The hospitality unit of measure ('one bite' — famously non-binding). Also لقمة عيش — the bite of bread one works for; a whole economy in two words.

example.en: Hospitality here isn't optional — it's a duty.

items.note: The system itself: قهوة الضيافة is the cup that cannot be (finally) refused. From the same ض-ي-ف as ضيف — the guest and the feeding of the guest are one root.

blocks.title: I survived the dinner
blocks.brief: A son-in-law reports from the front line of his in-laws' hospitality: the salad barrage, the maqluba ceremony, the mother-in-law's mathematics of 'you've eaten nothing.' Comedy — and every taste word from this lesson, live.
preQuestions: What was his plan going in — and how long did it last?
What happened when he said بكفي?
What state did he go home in?

transcript.speaker: الصهر
transcript.ar: مبارح كان عنا عزومة عند أهل مرتي.
transcript.en: Yesterday we had a dinner at my in-laws'.

transcript.speaker: الصهر
transcript.ar: قلت لحالي: لقمة وحدة وبمشي. ههه.
transcript.en: I told myself: one bite and I'm out. Haha.

transcript.speaker: الصهر
transcript.ar: بلشنا بالشوربة والسلطات — عشر صحون سلطة عالأقل.
transcript.en: We started with soup and salads — ten plates of salad, minimum.

transcript.speaker: الصهر
transcript.ar: بعدين وصلت المقلوبة. قلبوها قدامنا زي الاحتفال.
transcript.en: Then the maqluba arrived. They flipped it before us like a ceremony.

transcript.speaker: الصهر
transcript.ar: قلت بكفي — حماتي قالت: شو هالحكي، لسا ما أكلت إشي!
transcript.en: I said enough — my mother-in-law said: nonsense, you've eaten nothing!

transcript.speaker: الصهر
transcript.ar: حطتلي نص الصينية. والله نص الصينية.
transcript.en: She loaded half the tray onto my plate. I swear — half the tray.

transcript.speaker: الصهر
transcript.ar: وبعد كل هاد، كنافة وقهوة سادة.
transcript.en: And after all of that: knafeh, and bitter coffee.

transcript.speaker: الصهر
transcript.ar: رجعت عالبيت شبعان لأسبوع. الله يعطيهم العافية.
transcript.en: I went home sated for a week. God give them strength.

questions.why: One bite and out. The ههه that follows tells you how that went.
The flip IS the dish — that's why it's named 'the upside-down one.'
The official exchange rate: half a tray equals 'nothing.'
شبعان لأسبوع — sated on a geological timescale. The عزومة won, as it always does.

items.en: What's that delicious smell! What are you cooking?
The food is delicious — bless your hands.
The soup is a bit salty — add some water.
Take a small bite — just try.
I've eaten a lot — I'm full.
Lemon is sour and honey is sweet.

points.ar: أزكى من، أحلى من، أطيب من
points.explanation: Comparison is the أفعل template + من: زاكي → أزكى من, حلو → أحلى من. Drop the من for the superlative: أزكى كنافة بالدنيا. The national sport — food arguments — runs entirely on this pattern, and Nablus always wins.

examples.ar: كنافة نابلس أزكى من كل إشي.
examples.en: Nablus knafeh is tastier than everything.

examples.ar: أكل البيت أطيب من أكل برة.
examples.en: Home cooking beats eating out.

points.explanation: Wonder is شو + هالـ: what-is-this-smell! Unit 1's شو, promoted from question to applause. Fully sarcasm-capable, like every good exclamation — tone decides whether the عزومة is being praised or surveyed in horror.

examples.ar: شو هالريحة يا تيتا، فتحتي مطعم؟
examples.en: What is this smell, grandma — did you open a restaurant?
What a feast — a hundred dishes on the table!

items.story: ṭ-ʕ-m: the taste root, and Hebrew's bonus meaning — מה הטעם, 'what's the point.' Arabic keeps طعم on the tongue; Hebrew lets it wander into reasons. Both started at the same table.
r-w-ḥ: smell, wind, spirit — ريحة، ريح، روح and ריח، רוח. The same root breathes through noses, weather, and souls in both languages. The musakhan's ريحة is, etymologically, its soul traveling.
ś-b-ʕ: sated. From שובע ימים to شبعان لأسبوع — fullness, of food or of years, is one shared root. At a Palestinian table you'll discover its outer limits empirically.
m-l-ḥ: salt and its adjective, identical twice over. Bread-and-salt (عيش وملح / ברית מלח) seals loyalty in both traditions — sharing this root's referent has meant peace for a very long time.

lessons.title: Review & free listening
lessons.canDo: I can follow real Palestinians arguing about food — the dishes, the comparatives, the pride — at full street speed.

blocks.body: The souq, the money, the coffee ritual, the pantry, the senses. Now the exam Palestinians give each other daily: what is THE national food? Real people, three minutes, every dish from Lesson 4 — and the comparatives from Lesson 5 deployed as weapons.

blocks.title: Real street: the national food
blocks.brief: The Ask Project asks Palestinians to name the national dish — three minutes of مقلوبة versus مسخن partisanship, with حمص lobbying from the side. Short answers, full speed, and the lesson-5 comparatives (أزكى، أطيب) drawn like swords. You know every dish named; prove it.
preQuestions: Count the dishes you recognize: مقلوبة؟ مسخن؟ حمص؟ ملوخية؟ Which one wins the straw poll?
Listen for the comparatives — أزكى من، أطيب — Lesson 5's grammar, weaponized in the wild.
At least one speaker explains WHY a dish is national — catch one full reason and you've passed the unit.

No change on me — put it on the tab.

items.en: The guest won't eat until we say tafaddal.

items.ar: زيت السنة الجديدة بنزل بعد ____ الزيتون.
items.en: The new oil comes after the olive harvest.
Bitter coffee for grandpa, sweet for the kids.
Bon appétit! — (the reply:) on your heart.
